power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Mental health problems represent a major global challenge, with access to appropriate care for children and adolescents remaining severely limited.
Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) can offer scalable, accessible support beyond traditional clinical settings.

Despite a constantly growing number of youths DMHIs, the evidence base is constrained, due to a lack of replication and follow-up studies, scarce side-effect examination, and heterogeneous designs and characteristics.
This is particularly concerning regarding young people as a vulnerable population.
Knowledge of intervention processes is important to advance the field of DMHIs, while this topic is under researched in both DMHIs and traditional interventions for youth.
Reaching full potential of DMHIs for youth requires an integrated research and development approach.

We consulted experts from multiple disciplines, including youths psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists, computer scientists and ethicists specializing in digital mental health, to integrate the current state of knowledge into a conceptual framework.

The conceptual framework "From Lab to App (and Back)" emphasizes continuous exchange between DMHI research and development, with participatory collaboration, embedded ethics, and science communication relevant in all stages.
We outline that DMHIs are particularly well suited to generate insight into mechanisms of change and discuss key factors in DMHIs for youth.

Furthermore, we address the need for more unified conceptualizations and standardized reporting and illustrate a working intervention process model for youths DMHIs to induce an overarching research agenda.
Overall, the framework provides a structured pathway toward scientifically rigorous and clinically meaningful digital innovation in youth mental health research and practice.
Approximately half of all mental disorders begin during adolescence [1, 2], highlighting a great need for evidence-based mental health interventions for youth.

text.text: However, even in high income countries, a significant proportion of affected youth receive no mental health support, with fewer than 50% accessing services [3] and up to 61% reporting difficulties obtaining treatment [4].

text.text: Barriers for access to mental health interventions include individual barriers (e.g., self-stigma), social barriers (e.g., limited knowledge in family's about mental health and services) and structural barriers (e.g., financial constraints, long waiting lists, institutional stigma) [5] [6] [7] [8].

text.text: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) appear promising to oppose some of the barriers -they are considered easy to access and cost-effective, might enhance acceptance of seeking support [9], and might enhance ecological validity of treatments.

text.text: For instance, virtual reality can be used to simulate realistic scenarios [10], mobile apps can transfer therapy into daily life [11], and gamification can enhance motivation and compliance [e.g.12].

text.text: These advantages, along with daily use of technologies, have driven the development of numerous DMHIs for youth.
There are preliminary promising findings on positive effects of DMHIs on youth well-being and user satisfaction across various mental health conditions [13, 9, [14] [15] [16].

text.text: However, there is an alarming gap between the availability of DMHIs in app stores and their evidence [17, 18].
text.formatted: However, there is an alarming gap between the availability of DMHIs in app stores and their evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>.

text.text: On the one hand, DMHIs have high potential to help youth who are significantly underserved.
On the other hand, there is a clear need to advance research on DMHIs for youth, with special attention to the vulnerabilities of minors.
Resolving this gap is challenging because DMHIs form a heterogeneous group of interventions that are technology-based or -supported.
The most common forms for youth are apps followed by telemedicine [19].
text.formatted: The most common forms for youth are apps followed by telemedicine <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Here, the primary recipient can vary (e.g., parental trainings vs. childcentered approaches).
While DMHIs following a caregiver-focused approach show promising effects, e.g., [20, 21], less is known about interventions with the child as the primary recipient.
text.formatted: While DMHIs following a caregiver-focused approach show promising effects, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>, less is known about interventions with the child as the primary recipient.

text.text: DMHIs also differ in design and targets.
With a variety of possible implementations, the challenge is to identify the best fit between DMHI characteristics and a specific use case.
For example, a DMHI targeting school anxiety within a school setting should consider device accessibility due to smartphone bans at schools and peer or teacher presence during use.
In contrast, an intervention for specific phobia in a mental health center may involve virtual reality and therapist involvement.

When evaluating DMHIs, this heterogeneity leads to high variations in study designs, measurements, insufficient reporting of clients' characteristics, as well as a deficient description and non-uniform taxonomy of DMHIs, especially regarding the role of human support [16].
text.formatted: When evaluating DMHIs, this heterogeneity leads to high variations in study designs, measurements, insufficient reporting of clients' characteristics, as well as a deficient description and non-uniform taxonomy of DMHIs, especially regarding the role of human support <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: One critical prerequisite for examining the effects of different interventions is a common language.

Pineda and colleagues propose a useful taxonomy based on technology and human contact: (1) provider-administered, (2) provider-administered with blended digital adjuncts, (3) self-help with human support, and (4) fully automated self-help (see [22]).

text.text: To date, both provider-administered (e.g., videoconference-delivered [23]) and self-help DMHIs (e.g., internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy with human support [13], gaming intervention with human support [24]) have demonstrated efficacy.

text.text: There is some initial evidence for higher efficacy with more client-provider interaction [25].
text.formatted: There is some initial evidence for higher efficacy with more client-provider interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, conversational AI agents, which provide synchronous interaction in fully automated self-help DMHIs, show medium-tolarge effects in adolescents and young adults with depressive symptoms [26].
text.formatted: Interestingly, conversational AI agents, which provide synchronous interaction in fully automated self-help DMHIs, show medium-tolarge effects in adolescents and young adults with depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: With a few exceptions [e.g.27], studies designed to provide evidence on the effectiveness of a specific DMHI, like randomized controlled trials (RCTs), are mostly found for non-commercial DMHIs [18].
text.formatted: With a few exceptions [e.g.27], studies designed to provide evidence on the effectiveness of a specific DMHI, like randomized controlled trials (RCTs), are mostly found for non-commercial DMHIs <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: DMHIs widely available in the app stores, however, have a documented lack of evidence [17].
text.formatted: DMHIs widely available in the app stores, however, have a documented lack of evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Existing studies are mostly limited to short time periods, specific programs, settings, and target groups.
Evidence for long-term effects is scarce and mixed [28, 9].
text.formatted: Evidence for long-term effects is scarce and mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: A recent review on mental health apps reported that final assessments in RCTs occurred, on average, less than three months post-randomization and highlighted a substantial lack of replication studies [18].
text.formatted: A recent review on mental health apps reported that final assessments in RCTs occurred, on average, less than three months post-randomization and highlighted a substantial lack of replication studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: This might result from a trend to develop novel DMHIs, rather than refining, disseminating, and comprehensive evaluating existing ones [18].
text.formatted: This might result from a trend to develop novel DMHIs, rather than refining, disseminating, and comprehensive evaluating existing ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Adverse emotional and behavioral effects, as well as dropout, remain largely understudied, particularly in youth [13, 18, 29].
text.formatted: Adverse emotional and behavioral effects, as well as dropout, remain largely understudied, particularly in youth <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: We propose a conceptual framework advancing the field through a "from lab to app (and back)" approach, namely the continuous synergistic exchange between research and development, aiming to enhance evidence and to maximize stakeholder acceptance (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: We propose a conceptual framework advancing the field through a "from lab to app (and back)" approach, namely the continuous synergistic exchange between research and development, aiming to enhance evidence and to maximize stakeholder acceptance (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The framework emphasizes a continuous, synergistic exchange between DMHI research and development to enhance user acceptance and strengthen the empirical evidence base.

DMHI development and evaluation operate as collaborative processes, supported by science communication, embedded ethics, and participatory collaboration, which enhance each stage as well as the exchange between them.

Knowledge, innovations, and publicly available evidence generated through this process may be transferable to traditional intervention settings, extending impact beyond the digital context to support child and adolescent mental health more broadly.
In this context, DMHIs can be seen as a dynamic system in which multiple components interact to support a child's transition from a present state toward a desired future state [30].
text.formatted: In this context, DMHIs can be seen as a dynamic system in which multiple components interact to support a child's transition from a present state toward a desired future state <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: At its core are the structural (e.g., visual design, cover story) and functional components ("features", e.g., exposure to a prospective self by touching the screen to connect with a future-self avatar) of the specific DMHI [31].
text.formatted: At its core are the structural (e.g., visual design, cover story) and functional components ("features", e.g., exposure to a prospective self by touching the screen to connect with a future-self avatar) of the specific DMHI <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: While both types of components indirectly influence intervention progress, for instance, via user engagement [32, 33], the features are conceptualized as potential active ingredients that can drive change more directly.
text.formatted: While both types of components indirectly influence intervention progress, for instance, via user engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>, the features are conceptualized as potential active ingredients that can drive change more directly.

text.text: The process is characterized by mechanisms of change, mediators, and moderators.
Mechanisms of change are internal processes that translate an intervention into actual improvements.
Mediators are empirically testable variables that explain how or why change occurs, whereas moderators specify for whom and under which conditions the intervention is effective [30].
text.formatted: Mediators are empirically testable variables that explain how or why change occurs, whereas moderators specify for whom and under which conditions the intervention is effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Surrounding these core processes are social factors, such as the digital working alliance [34, 35], caregiver involvement [36, 37], and broader human support, which can be shaped by specifically designed DMHI components, and might strengthen or weaken an intervention's impact.
text.formatted: Surrounding these core processes are social factors, such as the digital working alliance <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35]</ref>, caregiver involvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37]</ref>, and broader human support, which can be shaped by specifically designed DMHI components, and might strengthen or weaken an intervention's impact.

text.text: For example, a child's commitment and accountability may be shaped by the involvement of caregivers [37].
text.formatted: For example, a child's commitment and accountability may be shaped by the involvement of caregivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: The therapeutic process is embedded within a broader context of environmental influences, extra-therapeutic factors, and social networks, including supportive or stigmatizing norms.

Together, these interconnected elements illustrate how change emerges from the interplay between designed intervention components, individual psychological processes, interpersonal dynamics, and the broader environment.
For a visualization of the described process model, see Figure 3.
text.formatted: For a visualization of the described process model, see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: This model was developed based on a previously proposed model for depression-focused DMHIs [30] and requires adaptation in future studies.
text.formatted: This model was developed based on a previously proposed model for depression-focused DMHIs <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> and requires adaptation in future studies.

text.text: For instance, commitment and supportive accountability as well as user engagement are considered critical for DMHIs, yet knowledge remains limited.

Indeed, recent accounts of digital working alliance indicate that applicationinduced accountability might not only be important in DMHIs with human support [30, 38], but also in self-help DMHIs, however, evidence is scarce [39, 40].
text.formatted: Indeed, recent accounts of digital working alliance indicate that applicationinduced accountability might not only be important in DMHIs with human support <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38]</ref>, but also in self-help DMHIs, however, evidence is scarce <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40]</ref>.

text.text: For the investigation of mechanisms of change in DMHIs, it is key to examine the intervention process in addition to the intervention outcome.
This approach has rarely been adopted for DMHI research in children and adolescents.
Even in classical face-to-face settings, our understanding of mechanisms of change in child and adolescent psychotherapy remains limited [30, 41].
text.formatted: Even in classical face-to-face settings, our understanding of mechanisms of change in child and adolescent psychotherapy remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>.

text.text: Strategies to address this include closely replicating face-to-face interventions digitally or adapting adult DMHIs for younger populations.
These strategies risk missing the unique opportunities digital interventions offer for youth.

Indeed, the early stage of DMHIs offers a unique chance to establish a collaborative, structured research agenda that identifies key factors and mechanisms in youth-focused and traditional interventions, guiding future development [30].
text.formatted: Indeed, the early stage of DMHIs offers a unique chance to establish a collaborative, structured research agenda that identifies key factors and mechanisms in youth-focused and traditional interventions, guiding future development <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: To uncover mechanisms of change, study designs must go beyond simple pre-post comparisons.
The literature recommends longitudinal studies with at least three measurement points to meaningfully assess mediators [30].
text.formatted: The literature recommends longitudinal studies with at least three measurement points to meaningfully assess mediators <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Intervention component studies examine intervention processes by isolating specific effects through varying individual components while keeping others constant.
This approach is preferably conducted as an RCT to provide robust effect size estimates [30].
text.formatted: This approach is preferably conducted as an RCT to provide robust effect size estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: We argue that DMHIs offer strong potential for research on mechanisms of change in child and adolescent therapeutic processes.
Due to their location-independent nature, they can reach larger sample sizes in more diverse samples.

Further, unlike face-to-face interventions, which struggle with standardization due to high interactivity, DMHIs provide a major advantage: their content is typically standardized and easily tracked [30].
text.formatted: Further, unlike face-to-face interventions, which struggle with standardization due to high interactivity, DMHIs provide a major advantage: their content is typically standardized and easily tracked <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: We recommend using transdiagnostic scales to enable pooled analyses of raw data across diverse study populations.
These scales can be applied across sites and modeled with study-and site-specific covariates in multilevel approaches [42], creating opportunities for systematic research beyond individual studies.
text.formatted: These scales can be applied across sites and modeled with study-and site-specific covariates in multilevel approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>, creating opportunities for systematic research beyond individual studies.

text.text: A particularly important consideration in child and adolescent DMHIs is the developmentally sensitive implementation of components, as the youth's developmental stage and prior experiences act as a key moderator of intervention effects.
While some components may not meaningfully contribute to the intervention process and can be considered inactive, others actively support change and are referred to as active ingredients or features.
Functional components are intentionally designed to serve as such active ingredients.

These include specific therapeutic techniques grounded in established theoretical frameworks (e.g., cognitive restructuring, exposure) as well as common factors relevant across therapeutic approaches and disorders (e.g., problem activation, motivation clarification).
DMHI components may further influence cognitive and affective mediators, thereby promoting change.
In addition, human support and caregiver involvement represent important influencing factors in youth DMHIs.

These factors may operate as contextual influences or can also be explicitly supported or facilitated as part of the DMHI itself through dedicated features (e.g., guidance, feedback, caregiver modules), thereby shaping commitment, engagement, and intervention outcomes.

Moreover, the working alliance is an important factor, which functions as both an active ingredient and a mediatorestablished through DMHI components and potentially human support, it influences engagement as well as mechanisms of change.

The model conceptualizes the therapeutic process as embedded within a broader context that encompasses extra-therapeutic and environmental factors, such as stressors, individual life circumstances, social networks, and normative influences.
Cognitive and Affective Mediators.
Cognitive mediators (e.g., self-efficacy, inhibitory control) represent the largest group of mediators that have been assessed for DMHIs.

Additionally, affective mediators (e.g., emotion regulation) so far show the highest proportion of significant associations with DMHI outcomes, albeit this is based on a limited number of studies [43, 44].

text.text: Intuitively, digital working alliance might differ significantly from traditional interventions.
DMHIs might lack some of the emotional responsiveness and nuanced understanding that face-toface interventions offer.

However, there is novel experimental evidence in adults that AIgenerated empathetic responses are perceived as more compassionate and responsive than human generated responses, and that conversational AI can establish closeness better than human interaction partners (interestingly, humans still prefer to receive empathy from humans than from AI agents) [76] [77] [78].

text.text: However, DMHIs may feel judgement-free, offering around-theclock availability and a sense of control, especially for those hesitant to seek traditional therapy.
There is evidence that digital alliance can be established successfully in guided [79, 80], but also in fully automated self-help DMHIs [81] in youth, and might reduce risk of drop-out [82].

text.text: To date, empirical work on digital working alliance in youth is scarce and diverse in scope and methods, and complicated by the fact that our understanding about mechanisms of working alliance in classical child psychotherapy remains scarce [34, 71, 83, 84].

text.text: Moreover, studying digital working alliance in youth remains challenging due to inconsistent measurements and the lack of validated tools, particularly for self-help DMHIs targeting children.

Last, we must not only consider possibilities to enhance digital alliance, but also keep in mind potential risks: there is evidence that excessive attachment and parasocial relationships, for example, to conversational AI, may lead to social withdrawal and loneliness, emotional dependence, or unrealistic expectations of the AI's capabilities [89].

text.text: Youth, their families, and professionals are embedded within social structures and contexts that shape how they feel, think, and behave throughout the intervention process.

For instance, in a qualitative study exploring motivational aspects related to completing unpleasant DMHI tasks, children frequently reported being motivated by a desire to follow their caregivers' instructions or to avoid their disapproval, whereas some adolescents named peer comparisons or general social expectations as motivating factors [96].

text.text: Importantly, whether and how caregiver involvement is beneficial might vary as a function of clients' age: Systematic caregiver involvement through specific DMHI features (e.g., specific modules on how to support therapeutic exercises) may be fruitful for younger children due to their limited experience in handling technology, as well as due to less mature cognitive, linguistic, and self-regulation abilities.

Drop-out rates in youth psychotherapy are high -around 60% [101] [102] [103] -and DMHI tools generally show low uptake [104].

text.text: DMHIs use technologies that may support the promotion of health (e.g., by ameliorating symptoms), while causing potential aversive effects at the same time (e.g., overly strong emotional dependence on a digital agent) e.g., [108] [109] [110].

text.text: Thus, careful consideration of (unintended) risks is key in DMHI development for children and adolescents, to avoid diminishing the enriching potential of DMHIs through undesirable outcomes.

text.text: DMHIs offer both opportunities and challenges in this regard.

They can contribute to stigma reduction through improved access, enhanced privacy, increased flexibility, user-driven engagement, and greater mental health awareness and literacy [126] [127] [128] [129] [130].
text.formatted: They can contribute to stigma reduction through improved access, enhanced privacy, increased flexibility, user-driven engagement, and greater mental health awareness and literacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">[126]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">[127]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">[128]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">[129]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">[130]</ref>.

text.text: However, DMHIs technical solutions, such as gamification elements intended to boost engagement, also risk inadvertently exacerbating stigma through unintended exposure of personal data and data tracking, as well as through increased visibility of therapeutic activities to others (e.g., frequent app use, notifications) and through potentially heightened disorder presentation resulting from reinforced illness identity (e.g., excessive engagement with disorder-related content) [131] [132] [133].

text.text: Yet, we have a limited empirical understanding of how digital environments shape stigma processes in youth populations.
In addition, cultural, gender, and age-related factors shape how stigma is perceived and experienced, including in digitally mediated settings [105, 134, 135].
text.formatted: In addition, cultural, gender, and age-related factors shape how stigma is perceived and experienced, including in digitally mediated settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">[105,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">134,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">135]</ref>.

text.text: A key step toward addressing these gaps is the development and validation of psychometrically sound instruments to assess stigma in youth, yet such tools remain scarce and largely tailored to adults or specific contexts, limiting their applicability to digital settings.
Thus, it is necessary, as in other interventions, to comply with child-specific data protection laws (e.g., GDPR-K in the European Union, COPPA in the US).
Consent processes need to be designed in a transparent way for both guardians and minors.
Particularly for younger individuals, this requires an adaptation of language and presentation mode. [136, 137] Overcoming Barriers Embedded Ethics.

text.text: The interdisciplinary nature of DMHI-research and implementation requires institutionalized ethical guidance, since existing ethical principles of one specific field (e.g. medicine) alone cannot guarantee ethical technologies nowadays [138].
text.formatted: The interdisciplinary nature of DMHI-research and implementation requires institutionalized ethical guidance, since existing ethical principles of one specific field (e.g. medicine) alone cannot guarantee ethical technologies nowadays <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[138]</ref>.

text.text: Given the novelty and developmental dynamics of DMHIs, consequences are difficult to foresee and tend to materialize only fully once the technology has been fully implemented.
Accordingly, anticipation of ethical issues often remains highly speculative and dependent on an in-depth knowledge of new tech developments.
To address these challenges, we advocate for embedded ethics in DMHIs for children and adolescents.

Embedded ethics refers to the theory and practice of integrating ethical considerations into entire research and implementation processes by having ethicists, researchers, and developers working together to identify and address ethical issues via an iterative and continuous process [139] [140] [141].
text.formatted: Embedded ethics refers to the theory and practice of integrating ethical considerations into entire research and implementation processes by having ethicists, researchers, and developers working together to identify and address ethical issues via an iterative and continuous process <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">[139]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">[140]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">[141]</ref>.

text.text: The main goal is to promote the advancement of DMHIs that are ethically and socially responsible.
This requires interdisciplinary offers for practical guidance and regular interdisciplinary communication channels.
Participatory approaches, involving children, caregivers, and clinicians, are increasingly integrated into DMHI frameworks and promising to overcome barriers [31, [142] [143] [144].

text.text: This can ultimately improve equitable access and maximize the societal impact of evidence-based DMHIs for children and adolescents.
DMHIs have the potential to significantly improve the landscape of therapeutic support for youth mental health.
They hold potential in advancing our knowledge about active ingredients and mechanisms of change in child and adolescent psychotherapy.
However, evidence-based tech development is still in its infancy.

Our proposed framework "From Lab to App (and Back)" leverages synergies between research and DMHI development: that includes not only continuous interdisciplinary exchange between the different fields but also the integration of embedded ethics, participatory collaboration, and science communication across fields and work stages.

Intervention effects and processes should be investigated strategically to enhance knowledge on intervention processes in general and build an open evidence-based pool of design feature concepts facilitating therapeutic success.

This requires investigation, with respect to both the effects and directions of effects, and the examination of influential factors in a causal manner (e.g., multiple assessment time points, experimental studies).

Next steps include establishing reporting standards, refining classical concepts (e.g., working alliance) for youth-and DMHI-specific contexts, and adapting assessment tools for younger populations (e.g., for cognitive and affective mediators).

This presents a tremendous opportunity for our understanding of mechanisms of change in child and adolescent psychotherapy in general, through high-frequency data collection, trackable content and usage, and standardized, modular structures that support experimental designs.
Their variability allows study of engagement and user experience, while their location-independent nature facilitates larger samples for complex analyses.
Finally, stakeholder involvement in DMHI development can help surface emerging research priorities.

These advanfces could foster a research ecosystem in which digital mental health interventions are rigorously validated, developmentally attuned, and broadly accessible-ultimately contributing to evidence-based support for young people with mental health conditions.

text.text: Figure 1.
This figure illustrates the challenge of finding best-fitting DMHI characteristics for a specific use case.
The left side displays multiple factors that need to be considered for the intended use case.

The right side illustrates the variety of DMHIs characteristics in terms of: (1) choice of technology use, such as the delivery device and implementation forms; (2) choice of human contact, spanning different levels of human involvement and communication forms.
It further shows that the space between the choices can be fulfilled by implementing various features.
Figure2.
Conceptual framework of the "lab to app and back" approach for advancing DMHIs for children and adolescents.
The framework emphasizes a continuous, synergistic exchange between DMHI research and development to enhance user acceptance and strengthen the empirical evidence base.

DMHI development and evaluation operate as collaborative processes, supported by science communication, embedded ethics, and participatory collaboration, which enhance each stage as well as the exchange between them.

Knowledge, innovations, and publicly available evidence generated through this process may be transferable to traditional intervention settings, extending impact beyond the digital context to support child and adolescent mental health more broadly.
Figure 3.
Our model, adapted from Domhardt and Baumeister (2021), illustrates factors determining the intervention process of DMHIs for youth.
The process starts with the young person in their present state, including individual prerequisites, who seeks change and therefore engages with a DMHI.
These interventions comprise both structural and functional components, whose effects on outcomes vary depending on individual and contextual factors.
